images.title: Matching primes of 112 and 84
images.purpose: Show how to match the primes of 112 and 84 one to one to find the largest common subpart, 28.
images.composition: Two rows of prime tiles, 112 on top and 84 below, with matched tiles joined by short vertical links; a short result block on the right.
exact_structure: Top row: label 112 then exactly 5 teal #0072B2 tiles: 2, 2, 2, 2, 7.
Bottom row: label 84 then exactly 4 amber #E69F00 tiles: 2, 2, 3, 7.
Exactly 3 reddish purple #CC79A7 links: first 2 to first 2, second 2 to second 2, 7 to 7.
The two unmatched 2s in the top row and the 3 in the bottom row are greyed #6B7280.
Result block on the right, two lines: Common factors: 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28 and HCF = 2 × 2 × 7 = 28.
rejection: more or fewer than 3 links, or a link drawn from a third or fourth 2 of 112
the 112 row without exactly four 2s and one 7, or the 84 row without exactly two 2s, one 3 and one 7
images.takeaway: A common subpart can use a prime only as many times as both numbers have it; the biggest one is the HCF.
images.description: Prime tiles of 112 above prime tiles of 84, with two 2s and the 7 linked, giving common factors 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28 and HCF 28.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on common subparts of 112 and 84.
images.teaching_notes: Count the links: only two 2s can match because 84 has only two.

image_decisions.why: Linking matched primes shows why only two 2s can be shared.
